title: Logging & Distributed Tracing
tagline: Structured logs, log levels, correlation IDs, distributed tracing spans, and OpenTelemetry — following a request across every service it touches.

sections.content:
In a monolith, debugging is uncomfortable but manageable — you add a `console.log`, reproduce the problem locally, and grep the output. The entire story of a request lives in one process on one machine. In a **distributed system** — microservices, serverless functions, message queues, event-driven pipelines — a single user action can touch a dozen services running on different hosts, in different programming languages, writing to different log files in different time zones. When something goes wrong, you face a jigsaw puzzle: dozens of log streams, no obvious way to say which lines belong to the same request, and timestamps that may drift by hundreds of milliseconds across machines.

This is the **observability problem**, and it is one of the defining engineering challenges of modern cloud-native software. Three pillars address it: **logs** (what happened), **metrics** (how much/how fast), and **traces** (exactly how a request flowed). This chapter focuses on the first and third: structured logging and distributed tracing, and how they are wired together with **correlation IDs** and the **OpenTelemetry** standard.

**Structured logging** replaces free-text log lines with machine-readable JSON records, making logs searchable and aggregatable at scale. A log aggregator like Elasticsearch, Grafana Loki, or AWS CloudWatch Logs can then answer questions like "show me all requests from user 42 that took more than 500ms and returned a 5xx status" — across a billion log lines, in seconds. **Correlation IDs** are the glue: a UUID generated at the entry point of a request and threaded through every log line and outbound HTTP call, so you can retrieve the complete story of a single request across all services by filtering on one field.

**Distributed tracing** goes a step further: instead of just recording that something happened, it records the exact start time, end time, and parent-child relationship of every operation in the call graph — every HTTP call, database query, cache lookup, and message publish. The result is a flame graph that shows precisely where time was spent and exposes the structure of your distributed system. **OpenTelemetry (OTel)** is the open standard — a CNCF project — that unifies all three observability signals into a single vendor-neutral instrumentation layer, so you instrument your application once and choose your backend (Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb) by changing configuration, not code.

sections.title: The International Package Tracking System
sections.content:
When you order a parcel online from abroad, it receives a **tracking number** the moment the seller hands it to the courier. Every handler along the route — local post office, regional sorting hub, customs facility, international carrier, destination hub, last-mile delivery van — scans that number and records a timestamped event: 'accepted at origin post, 2024-03-15 09:14 UTC', 'departed sorting facility, 09:47', 'cleared customs, 14:22', 'out for delivery, 08:11 next day'. If the parcel is late, you enter the tracking number on the courier's website and immediately see a complete timeline: which step added unexpected delay, whether it was stuck at customs, or whether it simply has not been scanned yet.

**The tracking number is the correlation ID** (or trace ID in distributed tracing terminology). Each physical location that handles the parcel is a **service** in your distributed system. Each scan event is a **structured log line** — machine-readable, timestamped, including the parcel ID, location code, status, and operator ID. The delay measurement between scans is a **span duration**. The complete chain of scans from origin to delivery is the **trace**: a comprehensive picture of the parcel's journey through the distributed logistics network.

**Structured logs** are those machine-readable scan events. Contrast them with an old-fashioned human-written note: 'parcel received somewhere, mid-morning, looks fine'. That note is useless for a computer to process. A structured log record — `{"event":"parcel.received","tracking_id":"abc123","facility_code":"SIN-HUB-02","timestamp":"2024-03-15T09:14:00Z","operator_id":"op-77","weight_kg":1.2}` — can be aggregated, filtered, and joined with records from every other facility automatically.

**OpenTelemetry** is the standardised scanner hardware and data format agreed upon by all carriers: every facility uses the same API, the same data schema, and the same protocol for uploading events to the central tracking portal. Before this standard existed, each carrier had its own proprietary system and you could not track a parcel that crossed carriers. OTel solves exactly that problem for microservices: regardless of whether a service is written in Node.js, Python, Java, or Go, the telemetry it emits looks the same to the aggregation backend.

sections.title: Structured Logging: From Free Text to Machine-Readable JSON
sections.content:
The fundamental shift in structured logging is from writing for humans to writing for machines — while keeping human readability as a secondary goal achievable via formatting tools.

**Unstructured (bad for production):**
```
2024-03-15 14:22:01 INFO User 42 purchased item 7 for $29.99 in 312ms
```
To extract the user ID from this, you write a regex like `User (\d+)`. Regexes break when someone changes the log message text. Querying 'all purchases over $50' requires scanning every line. Correlating this line with lines from another service is nearly impossible.

**Structured (good for production):**
```json
{"level":"info","timestamp":"2024-03-15T14:22:01.334Z","service":"order-svc","traceId":"abc123","userId":42,"itemId":7,"amount":29.99,"durationMs":312,"event":"purchase.completed"}
```
This record is natively indexed by a log aggregator. You write SQL-like queries: `userId = 42 AND level = 'error'`, `AVG(durationMs) WHERE event = 'purchase.completed'`, `COUNT(*) WHERE amount > 50 GROUP BY date`. The `traceId` field links this log line directly to the distributed trace for the same request.

**Log Levels** form a severity hierarchy. Every serious logging library (pino, Winston, structlog, logrus, zap) implements the same scale:
- `DEBUG`: Verbose detail for developers — variable values, SQL queries, loop iterations. Always disabled in production; can flood a system with thousands of lines per second.
- `INFO`: Normal operational milestones — request received, user authenticated, order created, background job started/completed.
- `WARN`: Unexpected but recoverable — a downstream service timed out and the request retried successfully, a config value fell back to a default, a deprecated API was called.
- `ERROR`: A request or operation failed — the user gets an error response, an exception was uncaught, a job failed and will be retried later.
- `FATAL` / `CRITICAL`: The service cannot continue — database unreachable, out of memory, required config missing. Imminent crash.

The choice of level is a business decision: in many teams an ERROR feeds alerting that can wake an on-call engineer at 3am; a WARN does not. A DEBUG line consumes storage and costs money. Level discipline is a team convention that must be enforced in code review.

**Child loggers and context binding** are the implementation pattern that makes structured logging ergonomic. Rather than passing `correlationId` as a parameter to every function that logs, you create a child logger bound to the request context. Every call on the child logger automatically includes the bound fields — `correlationId`, `userId`, `requestPath` — in the output JSON without repetition in the calling code. Libraries like pino (`logger.child({...})`), structlog (bound processors), and zap (fields on a `With` logger) all support this pattern.

sections.title: Correlation IDs: Linking Logs Across Service Boundaries
sections.content:
A **correlation ID** (also called a request ID or trace ID) is a UUID or similar unique identifier that represents a single user-initiated request or business operation throughout its entire journey through your distributed system.

The rules are simple but must be followed consistently across every service:
1. **Generate once at the entry point.** The API gateway, load balancer, or the first service to receive the request generates the ID if none is present in the incoming headers.
2. **Accept and forward if present.** If an incoming request already carries a correlation ID header (e.g. `x-correlation-id` or the W3C standard `traceparent`), preserve it. Never overwrite an existing ID — you want one ID for the entire user action, not a new one at each service hop.
3. **Include it in every outbound request.** When your service calls another service — via HTTP, gRPC, message queue publish, or any other mechanism — include the correlation ID in the request. For HTTP, this means adding it as a header.
4. **Include it in every log line.** Bind it to the logger at the start of request processing so that all log lines for this request include the ID without any extra effort in business logic code.
5. **Return it in the response.** Include the correlation ID in the response headers and, for errors, in the error response body. This allows users and client-side logging to tie a failed request to specific server-side log lines — invaluable for support tickets.

**The W3C Trace Context standard** (`traceparent` and `tracestate` headers) has largely superseded ad-hoc correlation ID headers for HTTP-based systems. The `traceparent` header encodes the trace ID, parent span ID, and trace flags in a standard format: `00-{traceId}-{parentSpanId}-{flags}`. When all your services use an OTel SDK, this header is propagated automatically without any manual header forwarding code.

**The async boundary problem** is a subtle but important edge case. Correlation IDs propagate easily over synchronous HTTP calls, but async systems (message queues, event buses, batch jobs) require explicit encoding of the correlation ID in the message payload or metadata. When a service publishes to Kafka or SQS, the correlation ID must travel in the message headers or body, and the consuming service must extract and bind it before processing begins. Forgetting this in async pipelines is a common source of broken traces.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Several design decisions deserve attention. The `redact` config strips sensitive fields from every log record at serialization time — safer than relying on developers to remember which fields to omit. The correlation middleware prefers the W3C trace ID when one arrives, so logs and traces share a single identifier, and it validates the header format instead of trusting arbitrary input. The middleware uses `res.on('finish')` because `finish` fires once the response has been handed to the OS, giving an accurate `durationMs` (`close` also fires when a client aborts). The error response returns `req.correlationId` — the value actually in use, even when it was generated rather than received — so a support team can query all server-side logs for the failing request. Passing the error object as `err` lets pino's standard serializer capture the stack trace.

sections.title: Distributed Tracing: Spans, Traces, and the Flame Graph
sections.content:
Correlation IDs tell you which log lines belong to the same request, but they do not tell you *why* the request was slow or which service caused a failure. **Distributed tracing** solves this by recording precise timing data for every operation in the request's call graph.

The core vocabulary:
- **Trace**: The complete record of a single request's journey through your system, from the moment it enters at the edge to the moment the final response is sent. A trace has a globally unique **trace ID**.
- **Span**: One unit of work within a trace. A span has a **name** (e.g. `"HTTP POST /orders"`, `"db.query"`), a **start timestamp**, an **end timestamp** (implying a duration), a **span ID**, a **parent span ID** (null for the root span), and a set of **attributes** (key-value pairs carrying context like `user.id`, `db.statement`, `http.status_code`).
- **Root span**: The first span created for a trace, with no parent. Usually represents the inbound HTTP request at the edge service.
- **Child span**: A span created during the execution of a parent span. Represents a downstream call — another service, a database, a cache, a message queue publish.
- **Span events**: Point-in-time annotations on a span, like log lines attached to the span. Useful for recording discrete events within a long operation: `"cache.miss"`, `"retry.attempt"`, `"payment.authorized"`.
- **Span status**: OK, ERROR, or UNSET. Set to ERROR when an exception occurs, which causes the span to appear red in trace UIs.

The **parent-child relationship** is what makes tracing powerful. When Service A calls Service B, Service A creates a child span and includes the span ID in the outbound request headers. Service B extracts the parent span ID from the headers and creates its own span as a child of Service A's span. This happens automatically when all services use an OTel SDK with HTTP instrumentation. The result is a **trace tree** that exactly mirrors the call graph of your request.

The **flame graph** (also called a **waterfall view** or **Gantt chart** in trace UIs) displays this tree visually. Each span is a horizontal bar positioned on a timeline. The width of the bar is proportional to the span's duration. Child spans are indented below their parents. This view immediately reveals:
- **Sequential vs. parallel work**: spans arranged end-to-end indicate sequential calls; spans at the same vertical level that overlap indicate parallel calls.
- **The critical path**: the sequence of spans that determines the minimum possible request duration. Optimising a span off the critical path produces no improvement in user-perceived latency.
- **Outlier latency**: a span that is far wider than its siblings is the bottleneck.
- **Error propagation**: a red span shows which operation failed, and the parent spans show which higher-level operations were affected.

sections.title: OpenTelemetry: The Unified Observability Standard
sections.content:
Before OpenTelemetry, every observability vendor provided its own proprietary agent and SDK: Datadog's `dd-trace`, New Relic's agent, Zipkin's instrumentation, Jaeger's client libraries. Switching backends meant rewriting instrumentation code. Mixing vendors was painful. The community was fragmented.

**OpenTelemetry (OTel)** emerged from the merger of two earlier projects — OpenCensus (started at Google) and OpenTracing (a CNCF project led by LightStep, Uber, and others) — and is now the second-most-active CNCF project after Kubernetes. It provides:

**APIs**: Language-specific interfaces for creating spans, recording metrics, and emitting logs. The API is stable and intentionally minimal — enough to instrument your code without taking a dependency on any vendor implementation.

**SDKs**: The concrete implementations of the APIs, including sampling logic, context propagation, and exporters. You configure the SDK at startup; your instrumentation code only calls the API.

**Automatic instrumentation**: For many frameworks and libraries (Express, Django, Spring, gRPC, Kafka clients, database drivers), OTel provides auto-instrumentation that patches the library to emit spans and metrics without any code changes in your application. You add a package, configure it, and your dependencies are automatically traced.

**The OTel Collector**: A vendor-agnostic proxy daemon, deployed as a sidecar or a standalone service, that receives telemetry via the OTLP protocol, applies processing (sampling, attribute redaction, batching), and exports to one or more backends. The Collector decouples your application code from your backend choice — you always export to `localhost:4317` (the Collector), and the Collector fans out to Datadog, Jaeger, Tempo, or any combination simultaneously.

**OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol)**: The wire protocol used between SDKs and the Collector, and between the Collector and backends. Based on Protocol Buffers and supports gRPC and HTTP transports.

**Context propagation**: The mechanism for transmitting trace context across service boundaries. OTel defines propagators that inject and extract context from HTTP headers, Kafka message metadata, gRPC metadata, and other transports. The default propagator implements the W3C Trace Context standard (`traceparent` header), but Baggage propagation (for user-defined key-value pairs) and B3 (Zipkin's legacy format) are also supported.

**Sampling** is a critical operational concern. In a high-throughput system, recording every span for every request would be prohibitively expensive. OTel supports:
- **Head-based sampling**: The decision to sample a trace is made at the root span, before any downstream spans are created. Simple and low-overhead, but cannot make decisions based on what happens later in the trace (e.g. sample all traces that resulted in an error).
- **Tail-based sampling**: The Collector buffers all spans for a trace and makes the sampling decision after the root span completes, allowing "keep all errors" or "keep traces slower than 1 second" policies. More complex but more useful. Requires the Collector to hold spans in memory briefly.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Two span-processor modes matter operationally: `SimpleSpanProcessor` exports each span as it ends — handy for local debugging, too expensive for production — while `BatchSpanProcessor` buffers spans and sends them in batches, vastly reducing overhead. Passing `traceExporter` to `NodeSDK` gives you the batch processor automatically; the `SIGTERM` handler calls `sdk.shutdown()` so the last batch is flushed. The `ParentBasedSampler` wrapping a `TraceIdRatioBasedSampler` is the standard production setup: the ratio sampler's decision is a deterministic function of the trace ID, and child services honour the sampled flag in the incoming `traceparent`, so all spans of a trace are kept or dropped together. The `propagation.inject` call shows what auto-instrumentation does under the hood for `fetch` and `http`. (OpenTelemetry JS packages are renamed and consolidated from time to time — the concepts here are stable, but check the current package names for your SDK version.)

sections.title: Connecting Logs and Traces: The Unified Observability Picture
sections.content:
Structured logs and distributed traces are most powerful when they are **correlated** — when a log line can link directly to its trace, and a trace span can link directly to its log lines.

The connection is established by injecting the **trace ID and span ID** from the active OTel span into every log record emitted during that span's execution. When a user-facing error occurs, your log aggregator (Grafana Loki, Elasticsearch) shows the error log line with a clickable trace ID. Clicking it opens the trace in your tracing backend (Grafana Tempo, Jaeger), showing the full flame graph of the request. From the flame graph you can jump to the logs from any individual span. This bidirectional linkage is called **trace-to-log correlation** and is a key feature of the Grafana LGTM stack (Loki + Grafana + Tempo + Mimir). Metrics can join in too: **exemplars** attach a sample trace ID to a histogram bucket, so a latency spike on a dashboard links straight to an example slow trace.

The implementation requires:
1. The OTel SDK exposes the current trace ID and span ID via `trace.getActiveSpan().spanContext()`.
2. Your logging library's serializer (pino transport, Winston format, structlog processor) reads these values and includes them in every log record.
3. Your log storage backend (Loki, Elasticsearch) indexes the `traceId` field.
4. Your trace storage backend (Tempo, Jaeger) is configured as a data source in Grafana alongside Loki.
5. Grafana's correlation feature is configured to recognize `traceId` in Loki logs as a link to Tempo.

**The THREE PILLARS in practice:**
- **Logs**: 'What happened at 14:22:01 in the order service for request abc123'
- **Metrics**: 'The p99 latency of the /orders endpoint was 450ms in the last 5 minutes'
- **Traces**: 'For request abc123, the DB INSERT took 110ms, about 40% of the 280ms request'

Logs tell you *what*. Metrics tell you *how much* and alert you something is wrong. Traces tell you *where* and *why*. You start an incident response with a metric alert, use logs to find the affected requests, and use traces to understand the root cause.

sections.title: Common Mistakes, Edge Cases, and Production Pitfalls
sections.content:
**Logging sensitive data accidentally.** Structured logging makes it dangerously easy to log entire objects: `logger.info({ body: req.body })`. If `req.body` contains a password field, a credit card number, a Social Security Number, or an auth token, it is now in your logs — potentially stored for months and visible to everyone with log access. Always allowlist specific fields rather than spreading entire objects. Use the `redact` configuration in pino or equivalent in other libraries to strip known-sensitive paths at the serializer level as a safety net.

**Wrong log levels cause two problems.** Logging too much at INFO floods your log storage and buries real signals. Logging genuine errors at DEBUG means on-call engineers miss them. Level discipline must be enforced in code review. A useful heuristic: if it wakes someone up, it is ERROR; if it is worth investigating next week, it is WARN; if it is business-as-usual, it is INFO; if it is only useful with the code open, it is DEBUG.

**Clock skew in distributed systems.** Each host has its own system clock, which can drift relative to other hosts by milliseconds (or far more on a misconfigured host) even with NTP. When you correlate log lines from two services by timestamp, this drift can make events appear out of order. Traces are affected too: every span records wall-clock start and end times from the host that created it, so a child span can appear to start before its parent. Trace UIs use the parent-child structure to reason about ordering, and some (Jaeger, for example) apply clock-skew adjustment. For logs, rely on correlation IDs and causal structure rather than raw timestamp ordering; use tighter time sync (chrony, cloud time services, or PTP) where precise ordering matters.

**Context propagation breaks at async boundaries.** In Node.js, the OTel SDK uses `AsyncLocalStorage` to propagate the active span context through async operations (Promises, async/await). This works automatically for `await`-based code but can break with raw callback-based APIs, `EventEmitter` listeners, or worker threads. If spans appear as root spans when they should be children, a broken async context is the likely cause. The fix is to explicitly pass the context: `context.with(ctx, () => { ... })`.

**Sampling strategy affects data quality.** Head-based sampling at 10% means 90% of your traces are never recorded. In low-traffic systems, you may sample 100%. In high-traffic systems, errors are rare and you want to sample all error traces. Tail-based sampling in the OTel Collector solves this: buffer all spans for a trace, and once the root span completes, apply a policy: 'always keep errors, keep 1% of successful traces under 200ms, keep 10% of traces over 500ms'. This gives you complete coverage of interesting cases while controlling cost.

**Span cardinality explosions.** Span attributes are indexed by trace backends. If you include high-cardinality values (user IDs, order IDs, UUIDs) as span *names* rather than span *attributes*, trace backends like Jaeger index them as separate operations and the UI becomes unusable with millions of unique operation names. Always use descriptive but low-cardinality span names (`"db.query"`, `"HTTP POST /orders"`) and put high-cardinality values in attributes.

**Serverless functions need explicit flushing.** Lambda functions and similar platforms freeze the execution environment as soon as the handler returns, so spans still sitting in a batch buffer may never be sent, and `SIGTERM` handlers are not a reliable flush point. Use the OpenTelemetry Lambda layer (or AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), which runs a Collector as a Lambda extension, and force-flush the tracer provider before the handler returns (the Lambda wrapper does this for you). Initialisation also happens on every cold start, so keep the instrumentation set small to avoid adding cold-start latency.

**Brief history:** The concept of distributed tracing was pioneered by Google's **Dapper** system, described in a 2010 paper that became enormously influential. Twitter followed with **Zipkin** (open-sourced 2012), and Uber with **Jaeger** (open-sourced 2017, CNCF graduated). The **OpenTracing** project (2016) and **OpenCensus** (Google, 2018) both attempted to standardise the instrumentation API, but they were incompatible. After years of fragmentation, they merged in 2019 to form **OpenTelemetry**, which reached stable status for traces in 2021, metrics in 2022, and the logs data model in 2023. Today, every major cloud provider and observability vendor supports OTel natively, and the `traceparent` header is a W3C standard (Trace Context Level 1, W3C REC 2021).

**Interview and production insights:**
- 'What is the difference between a trace and a span?' — A trace is the entire request journey (one trace ID); a span is one unit of work within that trace (own span ID, parent span ID, start/end timestamps).
- 'Why use structured logging over printf-style logs?' — Machine-parseable fields enable filtering, aggregation, and joining at scale without regex fragility.
- 'Why does my service's span appear as a root span instead of a child?' — Context propagation failed: the upstream service did not forward `traceparent`, or the async context was dropped at a callback boundary.
- 'What is head-based vs. tail-based sampling?' — Head: decision made at root span creation; tail: decision made after root span completes, allowing error-aware policies. Tail sampling requires the OTel Collector.
- 'What does `pino.child({correlationId})` return?' — A new logger that inherits all parent config and automatically merges `correlationId` into every log record — DRY propagation without threading the ID through function parameters.
- 'How do you prevent logging PII?' — Use the `redact` option in pino / allowlist fields explicitly; never spread entire request/response objects into log records; run log-level audits in code review.

items: **Structured logging** emits JSON records rather than free-text strings, enabling log aggregators to filter, index, and aggregate log data by specific fields (userId, statusCode, durationMs) across billions of records without fragile regex parsing.

**Log levels** (DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR < FATAL) are a business convention, not just a technical setting — the choice of level determines who gets woken up at 3am and how much your log storage costs.

**Correlation IDs** are UUIDs generated at the system entry point and forwarded in every outbound request header and log line; they enable retrieval of the complete story of a single user action across all services from any log aggregator.

**Distributed tracing** records parent-child span trees with precise timings, producing a flame graph that reveals the critical path, the bottleneck service, and whether work is sequential or parallel — none of which is visible from logs alone.

**OpenTelemetry** provides vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs, auto-instrumentation, and the Collector daemon; instrument once with the OTel SDK and switch backends (Jaeger, Datadog, Honeycomb, Tempo) by changing Collector configuration, not application code.

**Trace-to-log correlation** links structured log lines and distributed trace spans via a shared `traceId` field, enabling bidirectional navigation between a log line and its flame graph — the full three-pillar observability picture.

**Common production pitfalls** to avoid: logging sensitive data (use `redact`), high-cardinality span names (use attributes instead), broken async context propagation, and naive head-based sampling that misses all error traces in low-error-rate systems.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of structured (JSON) logging over plain-text logging in a distributed system?
options: JSON log files are smaller on disk because JSON compresses better than plain text.
JSON logging is faster to write at runtime because the logger does not need to format a string.
Structured logs are machine-readable, enabling log aggregators to filter, index, and aggregate by specific fields such as userId or statusCode across billions of records.
Structured logs automatically redact sensitive fields like passwords before the records reach storage.
quiz.explanation: Plain-text logs require fragile regex to extract fields, and regexes break when message text changes. JSON records are natively parsed by aggregators like Elasticsearch and Loki, enabling precise queries — 'statusCode >= 500 AND userId = 42' — across enormous datasets without any parsing code.

quiz.question: Where should a correlation ID be generated in a multi-service system, and what must every downstream service do with it?
options: The entry point (API gateway or edge service) generates the ID if none is present; every downstream service accepts it from the incoming header and forwards it in all outbound requests and log lines.
The database generates a correlation ID when a transaction opens, ensuring all DB operations share the same ID.
Each service generates its own correlation ID independently so failures can be isolated per-service.
The frontend browser generates the ID and appends it as a URL query parameter on every API call.
quiz.explanation: The correlation ID must be identical for every service that handles a single user request. Generating at the entry point and forwarding via a standard header (x-correlation-id or traceparent) ensures all log lines across all services share one ID. Services that generate their own ID break the chain — you can no longer retrieve the full story of a request by filtering on one value.

quiz.question: In distributed tracing, what is the precise relationship between a trace and a span?
options: A span contains multiple traces grouped by time window.
A span is created by the client; a trace is created by the server when the request is processed.
A trace and a span are interchangeable terms — both refer to the same timed operation.
A trace is the complete record of a single request's journey; a span is one unit of work within that trace, identified by a span ID and a parent span ID that forms the call tree.
quiz.explanation: A trace has one trace ID and contains one root span plus zero or more child spans. Each span records a start time, end time, name, attributes, and a parent span ID (null for the root). The parent-child nesting is what produces the flame graph — showing the full call tree with precise timing at every level.

quiz.question: A checkout request produces this span tree: API Gateway (root, 300ms) → Order Service (280ms), which calls Inventory check (30ms) and Payment Service (240ms) in parallel; Payment contains a DB INSERT (200ms). Which span is on the critical path and is the bottleneck?
options: Inventory check (30ms) — it runs first and blocks the payment from starting.
DB INSERT (200ms) — it is the longest single span and the Payment Service cannot complete until it finishes.
API Gateway (300ms) — as the root span it determines the total request duration.
Order Service (280ms) — it is the largest child of the root span.
quiz.explanation: The critical path is the sequence of spans that determines the minimum possible request duration. DB INSERT (200ms) is inside Payment Service (240ms) which is inside Order Service (280ms). Reducing DB INSERT duration directly reduces Payment Service duration, Order Service duration, and the overall request time. The Inventory check runs in parallel with Payment and at 30ms is not a bottleneck.

quiz.question: What is the W3C `traceparent` header, and what information does it carry?
options: An authentication header that carries a service-to-service JWT token for inter-service authorization.
A deprecated Zipkin B3 header that OpenTelemetry replaced with OTLP.
A header that tells the receiving service which log level to use for the incoming request.
A standard header that carries the trace ID, the current span ID, and trace flags, allowing the receiving service to create its new span as a child of the sender's span.
quiz.explanation: The W3C Trace Context standard defines traceparent with format '00-{traceId}-{parentSpanId}-{flags}'. When Service B receives this header, the OTel SDK extracts the trace ID and parent span ID, creates Service B's span as a child, and the distributed trace tree assembles itself automatically without any application-level parent reference passing.

quiz.question: What log level is most appropriate for a database connection that failed on the first attempt but succeeded on the second retry, with no user-visible impact?
options: WARN — the situation was unexpected and signals instability worth monitoring, even though the request ultimately succeeded.
INFO — the operation ultimately succeeded, so it is a normal operational event.
DEBUG — retries are internal implementation details only relevant during development.
ERROR — any database failure must be logged as an error regardless of whether recovery succeeded.
quiz.explanation: WARN is for unexpected but recoverable situations. A retry that succeeds means the user was not affected, so ERROR would be misleading and might trigger unnecessary alerts. But the retry indicates instability — if retries are accumulating, it warrants investigation. DEBUG would make it invisible in production; INFO would not capture the 'unexpected' signal.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of the OpenTelemetry Collector in a production observability stack?
options: It generates synthetic load test traces to validate your tracing backend configuration.
It is a Grafana plugin that renders span flame graphs from raw OTLP data.
It is a vendor-agnostic proxy daemon that receives telemetry from applications via OTLP, applies processing such as sampling and attribute redaction, and exports to one or more backends.
It replaces the application-side SDK — you do not need to instrument your code if you deploy the Collector as a sidecar.
quiz.explanation: The OTel Collector decouples application instrumentation from backend choice. Applications always export to the Collector (usually localhost:4317); the Collector fans out to Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, or multiple backends simultaneously. Changing backends requires only Collector configuration changes, not code changes. The Collector also enables tail-based sampling, which requires buffering complete traces before making sampling decisions.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid using high-cardinality values like user IDs or UUIDs as span names in OpenTelemetry?
options: OTel SDKs enforce a maximum span name length of 64 characters, and UUIDs exceed this limit.
Trace backends index span names as operation types. High-cardinality span names create millions of unique operation entries, making the trace UI unusable and degrading backend performance.
High-cardinality span names cause the BatchSpanProcessor to drop spans when the buffer is full.
The W3C Trace Context standard prohibits non-ASCII characters in span names, and UUIDs contain hyphens.
quiz.explanation: Trace backends like Jaeger and Tempo build indexes over span operation names to power their UIs. If every span name is unique (e.g. 'order-a3f7b2c1', 'order-d8e4f091'), the index grows to millions of entries and becomes unusable. Span names should be low-cardinality descriptors ('db.query', 'HTTP POST /orders'). High-cardinality values like order IDs belong in span attributes, which are stored per-span but not indexed as operation categories.

quiz.question: What is the difference between head-based sampling and tail-based sampling in distributed tracing?
options: Head-based sampling samples the first N spans of each trace; tail-based sampling samples the last N spans.
Head-based sampling applies to HTTP traces; tail-based sampling applies to database and queue spans.
Head-based sampling is performed by the application SDK; tail-based sampling is performed by the storage backend after ingestion.

Head-based sampling makes the keep/drop decision at the root span before any child spans are created; tail-based sampling buffers all spans for a trace and decides after the root span completes, enabling policies like 'always keep error traces'.
quiz.explanation: Head-based sampling is simple and low-overhead but cannot make decisions based on outcomes — it cannot preferentially keep error traces because the error has not happened yet when the root span is created. Tail-based sampling in the OTel Collector buffers spans in memory until the root span completes, then applies policies: 'always keep errors', 'keep 1% of fast successful traces', 'keep 20% of slow traces'. This gives much better coverage of interesting cases at the same storage cost.

quiz.question: When a `pino` child logger is created with `logger.child({ correlationId, userId })`, what is the effect on subsequent log calls made through that child logger?
options: The child logger inherits the parent's configuration (level, transport, serializers) and automatically merges the bound fields into every log record without repeating them in each individual log call.
The child logger reduces the minimum log level to DEBUG for this request to capture all diagnostic information.
The child logger writes to a separate log file for this request to avoid mixing with other requests.
The child logger creates a new process-level context that persists beyond the current request, usable by background jobs.
quiz.explanation: A pino child logger is a shallow clone of the parent with additional bound bindings. Every call to child.info(), child.error() etc. automatically includes correlationId and userId in the output JSON — no manual threading of these values through function parameters. This is the DRY pattern for request-scoped logging: bind once at the middleware level, use everywhere in the request handler without repetition.
